seo.title: Karmic tail 18 6 6 compatibility: The Moon, then The Lovers twice
seo.description: Karmic tail 18 6 6 compatibility in a couple's destiny matrix: The Moon at the entry, The Lovers twice, and what A Midsummer Night's Dream reveals about it.

title: The 18-6-6 karmic tail in compatibility: a midsummer night's dream for two
short: The 18-6-6 karmic tail in destiny matrix compatibility is The Moon at the entry followed by The Lovers twice in a row. The oddity shows at once: the couple's shared task opens with a night card, and its middle and its goal are the same card. The answer is this: it is the tail of two people who enter love through mystery, imagination and a world of their own, and who have to learn to repeat their choice of each other by daylight — knowing the living person rather than the image the night painted.

sections.h2: A Midsummer Night's Dream: the play that stages the 18-6-6 tail
paragraphs: The play was written around 1595. Theseus, Duke of Athens, is waiting to marry Hippolyta, and the moon sets the date: the wedding is to be at the new moon. "But, O, methinks, how slow / This old moon wanes!" Theseus complains. By the same day young Hermia must give her answer: her father, Egeus, is giving her to Demetrius, but she loves Lysander. The law of Athens leaves her three roads: obedience, death or the convent. The lovers decide to run — at night, through the forest. Demetrius follows them, and Helena, who loves Demetrius, follows him.

The forest has masters of its own, Oberon, king of the fairies, and Titania, his queen, and they are quarrelling. Oberon sends Puck for a flower whose juice, laid on a sleeper's eyelids, makes him fall in love with the first creature he sees on waking. Puck muddles the Athenians, and in one night everything turns over: both young men now swear love to Helena, Hermia cannot understand what has happened, and Titania embraces the weaver Bottom, who wears an ass's head. At dawn hunting horns wake the four. The spells are lifted — all but one. Theseus overrules the father, and three weddings are held in the temple. At the feast the craftsmen perform "Pyramus and Thisbe", and one of the parts is played by the Moon itself.

Open the text and it is plainly a play about The Moon and The Lovers, quite literally. We counted the words in the spoken lines of all 37 plays in the MIT edition of Shakespeare: moon, moonshine and moonlight occur 45 times in the Dream, against 12 in The Tempest, which comes next. And no other play talks about eyes so densely: 65 times in sixteen thousand words. The moon and eyes — the light by which people look, and those who look.

Even the title carries the Moon. "’Tis Midsummer-moon with you" was what English speakers said to someone who had gone mad; Brewer's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable records the saying in its 1894 edition. In Shakespeare's own Twelfth Night, Olivia calls the antics of her love-struck steward "midsummer madness". And Theseus speaks the key to the play in the fifth act:
The lunatic, the lover and the poet / Are of imagination all compact.

Lunatic comes from the Latin luna — "moon-struck". The first two words of the famous speech are the first two cards of the tail: the moon-struck and the lover. Fyodor Tyutchev published his Russian version of this passage in 1833: "Lyubovniki, bezumtsy i poety / Iz odnogo voobrazhenya sliti" — lovers, madmen and poets, fused out of one imagination.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: The Moon, or what the couple wants together
paragraphs: The entry to the task is the point that holds the couple's shared desire and their common language. The play describes that language in its very first scene — through the mouth of someone who does not understand it. Egeus complains to the Duke about Lysander: "Thou, thou, Lysander, thou hast given her rhymes, / And interchanged love-tokens with my child: / Thou hast by moonlight at her window sung, / With feigning voice verses of feigning love". To the father this is deceit and witchcraft: "This man hath bewitch'd the bosom of my child". To the two of them it is a language nobody else speaks: verses, bracelets of hair, trinkets that mean something only to the two of them.

A couple with The Moon at the entry wants the same thing. A world of its own that outsiders cannot enter. Words only the two of them understand: nicknames, jokes, glances across the table. Night conversations after which the morning feels foreign. The feeling that the other understands without explanation and that every year reveals something new in them. Lisovskaya describes The Moon in a couple, on its bright side, in almost the same way: the two understand each other by intuition and guard each other's private space, and what holds them together is play and mystery.

The Moon even stands in the very name of the beginning. A honeymoon is, word for word, a moon of honey; in Russian, mesyats means both a month and the crescent in the sky. The first explanation of the word was left by Richard Huloet in his dictionary of 1552: the proverb so calls the newly married, who do not quarrel at first and love each other beyond measure, though it is already plain that this excess will ebb — "the likelihood of their exceadinge love appearing to aswage, ye which time the vulgar people call the hony mone". The moon got into the name because it changes. At the end of the play, watching Moonshine in the craftsmen's show, Hippolyta will say: "I am aweary of this moon: would he would change!" — and Theseus will reply that "he is in the wane; but yet, in courtesy, in all reason, we must stay the time". **The Moon at the entry is a phase, not a permanent state.** The couple's task begins where it wanes.

paragraphs.h3: When the same entry turns into resistance

paragraphs: The entry to the task stands on the line of tasks, so the same desire turns into resistance. The wish to protect the magic becomes a reluctance to speak plainly: important things are put off "so as not to spoil it". A question is replaced by a guess. Theseus described the mechanism more precisely than many psychologists: imagination, if it expects joy, sees joy's messenger, and "in the night, imagining some fear, / How easy is a bush supposed a bear!"

In a couple's life the bush looks like this. One is late to reply — by midnight the other already knows why, and that knowledge is worse than any truth. One is silent at dinner from tiredness — the other hears a verdict in the silence. The partner has not said a word yet, and the other already has a whole story with a beginning and an end. Among The Moon's tasks for a couple Lisovskaya names exactly this: jealousy and grievances born of invented stories, an image created at the start that later collapses, secrets that one day become weapons.

Shakespeare showed the price of such a bush — and showed it as comedy. In the fifth act the craftsmen perform "Pyramus and Thisbe", a story from Ovid's Metamorphoses. The lovers have agreed to meet at night by a tomb; Thisbe is frightened by a lion and drops her mantle, which the lion mauls with its bloody jaws; Pyramus finds the mantle, decides she is dead and stabs himself, and Thisbe dies over him. The whole tragedy is a single misread clue by moonlight. Pyramus even thanks the Moon "for thy sunny beams": he takes moonlight for daylight. The four, just back from the forest, laugh at the show — and fail to notice that they are watching the night they themselves barely survived.

paragraphs.h3: A forest that belongs to no one

paragraphs: The Moon in this tail has an oddity that only the numbers reveal. Each point of a couple is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, and the entry of a personal tail is always a multiple of three. So the 18 at the couple's entry can be formed in only three ways: 3 + 15 (The Empress and The Devil), 6 + 12 (The Lovers and The Hanged Man) or 9 + 9 (two Hermits). **Neither of the two brings a Moon of their own to the entry.** The forest belongs neither to Hermia nor to Lysander: it appears only when they leave the city together. In one such couple in four (26%) The Moon is formed by two Hermits — two people carrying lanterns. That is exactly how Shakespeare brought the Moon on stage: in the craftsmen's show it is played by a man with a lantern.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: the flower that confuses the choice
paragraphs: The passage of the play that fits the middle of the tail best is Oberon's account of where the magic flower came from. Cupid took aim at a maiden in the west, "But I might see young Cupid's fiery shaft / Quench'd in the chaste beams of the watery moon" — and the arrow fell on a little flower, "Before milk-white, now purple with love's wound". Love's arrow passed through moonlight and became a juice that changes what the eyes see. This is the tail's step from 18 to 6: The Lovers, having passed through The Moon.

The flower has a name: love-in-idleness, which the standard Russian translation by Tatiana Shchepkina-Kupernik renders as "Lyubov v prazdnosti". It is the wild pansy, and pansy comes from the French pensée, "thought"; in Hamlet Ophelia will say: "there is pansies, that's for thoughts". In Russian the flower is called anyutiny glazki — "Annie's little eyes". A thought dropped onto the eyes: falling in love has never been described more exactly. Helena says the same without any flower:
Love looks not with the eyes, but with the mind; / And therefore is wing'd Cupid painted blind.

Love looks with the mind, not the eyes, and that is why Cupid is painted blind. The Russian translation has Helena say "heart", but Shakespeare wrote precisely "mind": love sees what it has imagined. And further: love is called a child "Because in choice he is so oft beguiled".

The middle of the task is how the couple lives the road from shared desire to the main task. For 18-6-6 the road runs through choice, and the choice is not made once. Where to live and whose friends to spend Saturday with. Whose side to take when a mother calls. Whether to stay in or go out. Every such decision is a small "you or not you". Among the things that fill a couple with The Lovers, Lisovskaya names precisely shared decisions even in small matters — that is, the act of choosing together.

But here the choice is made by moonlight, and sometimes it gets tangled. Yesterday the partner seemed the best person on earth; today, a stranger. The one who adored suddenly cools and is sure reason brought them there; Lysander, under the juice, says just that: "The will of man is by his reason sway'd". After the night Hermia puts this state better than anyone: "Methinks I see these things with parted eye, / When every thing seems double." And Helena answers: "And I have found Demetrius like a jewel, / Mine own, and not mine own."

**"Mine own, and not mine own" is the formula of the tail's middle.** The partner is chosen but not owned; found but not possessed. The downside of The Lovers in Lisovskaya — jealousy, checking, suspicion — grows exactly from the attempt to make "mine" what also remains "not mine". A caveat: the swaps in the forest are the flower's work, that is, the work of perception. The Lovers in the tail do not mean a third person in the couple.

sections.h2: Main task: the same choice by daylight
paragraphs: The morning in the play begins with Theseus's question: "But speak, Egeus; is not this the day / That Hermia should give answer of her choice?" The night is over, and the tail's main task is stated plainly: to choose. A couple's main task is read mostly through its downside — what does not work for the couple and what it has to learn. For The Lovers on this point Lisovskaya sees several such tasks, and in the play each one has a scene of its own.

**To choose with your own eyes, not someone else's.** "I would my father look'd but with my eyes," says Hermia. "Rather your eyes must with his judgment look," the Duke replies. Lysander lists what stands in love's way, and Hermia reacts most bitterly to "the choice of friends": "O hell! to choose love by another's eyes." For a couple with this tail, other people's eyes come in many forms: a mother's "he's not the one", a friend who keeps count of the other's faults, a picture of someone else's happiness to measure one's own against. Lisovskaya calls this dependence on relatives; in the play it has a name — Egeus.

**To believe that you were the one chosen.** Abandoned in the forest, Helena says of herself: "No, no, I am as ugly as a bear". And when a minute later Lysander, under the juice, swears his love to her, she is not glad but offended: she decides she is being mocked. The task that Lisovskaya puts as love for oneself within the couple looks exactly like this: a person who is loved hears mockery in a compliment and keeps checking whether the choice has been cancelled. Sometimes one partner teaches this to the other.

**Not to turn insecurity into control.** That same night Hermia, deciding that Helena has stolen Lysander from her, flies at her friend. Helena cries "you puppet, you!", Hermia answers "thou painted maypole" and threatens that "my nails can reach unto thine eyes" — the quarrel is about height, that is, about who is worse than whom. The jealousy of The Lovers on its downside grows from insecurity, not from love, and in a couple it looks familiar: a read message thread, an interrogation about "who were you with", words that cannot be taken back.

**To love a person, not an image.** The lover, Theseus says, "Sees Helen's beauty in a brow of Egypt". Titania tells an ass, "Thou art as wise as thou art beautiful" — and the ass himself, Bottom the weaver, turns out soberer than the queen: "reason and love keep little company together now-a-days". Lisovskaya places idealisation among the tasks of The Lovers next to perfectionism: demanding a picture from the relationship and conformity to it from the partner.

paragraphs.h3: Two sixes: the night choice and the day choice

paragraphs: The middle and the main task of this tail are one card. The road and the goal coincide: to choose in order to choose. Lysander chooses Hermia twice — in Athens, under her window by moonlight, and in the morning after the forest, when the spell is lifted. It is the same person, but the second choice is made by daylight, after a night in which everything seemed double. **The hidden plot of 18-6-6 is not finding "the one" but choosing the one you have already chosen — now knowing them.**

With Demetrius Shakespeare is bolder: his spell is never lifted, right to the end of the play. He tells the Duke himself: "I wot not by what power,— / But by some power it is,—my love to Hermia, / Melted as the snow" — and at once: "Now I do wish it, love it, long for it, / And will for evermore be true to it." The play does not ask love to prove where it came from. It asks something else: that a choice made at night be confirmed by day, aloud and in front of others. For a couple this is an honest thought: a beginning does not have to be reasonable for what follows to be real.

The play has a line that readers usually skip, though it holds the way out of the tail. On waking, Demetrius calls the others to the temple: "And by the way let us recount our dreams." The four walk and compare what each of them saw. Later Theseus refuses to believe their story: "More strange than true". Hippolyta objects — and in the original her answer is stronger than in the familiar Russian translation:
But all the story of the night told over, / And all their minds transfigured so together, / More witnesseth than fancy's images / And grows to something of great constancy.

In plain prose: the whole story of the night, told over again, and all their minds changed together, testify to more than fantasy and grow into something very constant. In Shchepkina-Kupernik's translation Hippolyta speaks more softly — "it seems to me there is truth in this" — and the word constancy disappears. Yet here it is the key word. Waite gives The Moon reversed the meaning "inconstancy"; Juliet begs Romeo not to swear by "the inconstant moon". **Hippolyta names the opposite: a night told by two becomes constancy.**

Wen closes The Moon reversed with a similar formula — "everything that rises must converge". The night visions of the four converge into one story, and the story proves sturdier than any single vision. For a couple with the 18-6-6 tail this is a working method, not a metaphor: The Moon at the entry stops frightening once the night has been talked through aloud and the versions compared. In practice it looks like this:

ul: to tell each other the story of how it began — each their own version — and find where the versions differ;
to turn a guess into a question: not "that hurt" but "did that hurt?";
to call a bush a bush, aloud: "right now I'm afraid that…" — and let the other answer;
to leave room in the couple for mystery and play, but not for silence about what matters;
to choose aloud, in small things, remembering that choosing each other is repeated, not done once and for all;
not to measure the couple against other people's eyes — parents', friends', those on a screen.

sections.h2: The centre of the couple: a sleep in the forest or a whole world
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is "The atmosphere inside the couple" — what happens between the two when nobody is watching. Couples with the 18-6-6 tail have only two cards in the centre: The Hanged Man in 69.9% and The World in 30.1%.

**The Hanged Man** is the four lovers' sleep in the forest: between night and morning they lie on the grass, and everything is settled without them. Lisovskaya describes couples with The Hanged Man in the centre this way: they take a long time to enter a relationship, and marriage needs a push from outside. In the play the push comes from Theseus: "Egeus, I will overbear your will". And on the downside of the same card she names the power of parents over the couple — that is, Egeus, who came to the Duke demanding the law. Both sides of the centre are in one scene. There is arithmetic too: Lisovskaya allows repeated energies to be added up, and the tail's two sixes give 6 + 6 = 12 — the very Hanged Man that stands in the centre of seven couples out of ten.

**The World** is a card that never appears in the centre of a personal matrix, for any birth date: in the centre it arises only in a couple. Among couples with the 18-6-6 tail it comes from every couple of one combination of personal tails — 15-20-5 + 3-22-19 — and only that one. The atmosphere of such a couple is a whole world with its own weather. In Shakespeare this shows in the play's second couple, Oberon and Titania: their quarrel confuses the seasons, frost falls on roses, "the mazed world, / By their increase, now knows not which is which" — and Titania admits: "We are their parents and original." They make peace with a dance and a blessing of someone else's house. On the bright side of The World in the centre Lisovskaya sees full acceptance of the partner, much talk and compromise; on the downside, many secrets and illusions about the relationship. With The Moon at the entry this follows directly: a world for two is good as long as people live in it, not illusions alone.

sections.h2: The couple's values: Diana's cell and the Hermit's lantern
paragraphs: In the first scene the Duke lists what awaits Hermia if she does not submit to her father's choice: death or a vow at Diana's altar — "To live a barren sister all your life, / Chanting faint hymns to the cold fruitless moon." For the Romans Diana was a goddess of the moon. Solitude under a cold moon — that is the punishment for a choice of one's own.

In the matrix of a couple with the 18-6-6 tail these same two cards stand in "The couple's values" — the point read for what the union exists for and which road it should walk together: The Hermit in 64% of such couples, The Moon in 36%. What Athens threatens as a sentence turns out, for the couple, to be a value — only not instead of the union but within it. Each has their own time and place for solitude, and love is shown in deeds more than words — this is how Lisovskaya describes The Hermit in a couple. And to a couple with The Moon she advises accepting the partner's need to withdraw into themselves at times: it is a way to recover, not a lack of love.

Waite insists that The Hermit is not a card of "occult isolation": his beacon intimates that "where I am, you also may be". A lantern, not a wall. Shakespeare's Moonshine holds a lantern too: "This lanthorn doth the horned moon present". **The value of a couple with this tail is not to merge into one but to light the way for each other.**

sections.h2: Clues in Waite: inconstancy, a dog and marriage
paragraphs: The cards in the reading on this site are drawn in their own style. This section is about the Waite–Smith deck and Waite's book The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910).

Waite defines The Moon in a sentence Theseus could have spoken: "The card represents life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit". His divinatory list gives The Moon deception and error, and reversed: "Instability, inconstancy, silence". On the Waite–Smith card a dog and a wolf howl at the moon. In Shakespeare Moonshine comes on with a dog of his own — "this dog, my dog" — and in Puck's last song "the wolf behowls the moon".

Waite describes The Lovers on the Waite–Smith card as two figures "unveiled before each other". That is where the tail leads: from an image in the half-dark to two people who see each other uncovered.

One more clue lies in the numbers. Waite also gives The Lovers an older name: "The Lovers or Marriage". And his lists hold two more cards with the word marriage: the meanings of The Hierophant begin with "Marriage, alliance", and The Sun has "fortunate marriage". **In 52% of couples with the 18-6-6 tail one of the two sixes is formed from exactly these two cards:** The Sun in one partner and The Hierophant in the other give 19 + 5 = 24 → 6. In the combination 15-20-5 + 3-22-19 (30% of such couples) this is how the main task is formed; in 12-19-7 + 6-5-17 (22%), the middle. A wedding in the temple in the morning sun — the very ending of the play.

A couple's tail is worked out from two personal matrices. A person born on 09.05.1976 has the personal tail 3-22-19; a person born on 17.01.1976 has 15-20-5. This is the most common combination for 18-6-6: 30% of such couples. The points are added, and a sum above 22 is reduced by adding its digits.

The couple's middle is taken from the middles of the two personal tails, 22 and 20, not from the couple's two outer numbers. In this tail it happens to match the sum of the outer numbers (18 + 6 = 24 → 6), but it is still worked out separately.

The Moon at the entry here is one partner's Empress and the other's Devil. The main task is one partner's Sun (19) and the other's Hierophant (5): that very pair of Waite's "marriage" cards. The centre is 11 + 10 = 21, The World, which never occurs in a personal matrix. "The couple's values" is 9, The Hermit. "Image of the couple" is 8, Justice. And "What to create together" is 6, so The Lovers appear three times in this couple. Repeats, according to Lisovskaya, can be added: 6 + 6 + 6 = 18 — The Moon, the very card of the entry. The circle closes on itself.

sections.h2: How to recognise the 18-6-6 couple tail and what not to confuse it with
paragraphs: The compatibility calculator on this site works out a couple's tail from two birth dates for free. By hand it takes three steps: find both personal tails (entry, middle, main task), add entry to entry, middle to middle and task to task, and reduce any sum above 22.

The 18-6-6 tail occurs in roughly one couple in 67 (1.499%) and ranks 24th of the 97 couple tails. It is formed from six combinations of personal tails: most often 15-20-5 + 3-22-19 (30%), then 12-16-4 + 6-8-20 and 12-19-7 + 6-5-17 (22% each), 9-12-3 + 9-12-3 (12%), 9-15-6 + 9-9-18 (9%) and 9-3-21 + 9-3-21 (5%). In one such couple in six the partners' personal tails are identical — the two enter the forest by the same path. And neither partner has the personal tail 18-6-6 in any of the six combinations.

There are no other couple tails made of the same numbers: 18, 6 and 6 cannot be rearranged. There is, however, a personal 18-6-6 tail — for 3,001 birth dates since 1900. That is a different calculation with different roles for the points: a personal tail speaks about one person, a couple's tail about a task that appears only for two. Texts for one do not carry over to the other.

**M · Entry to the task — 18, The Moon.** What the couple wants together: a world of its own that outsiders cannot enter, understanding without words, a shared secret. The same entry easily turns into resistance: things left unsaid, guesses instead of questions, fears grown in the half-dark.
**N · Middle of the task — 6, The Lovers.** How the couple travels the road: through a choice that has to be made again and again — in small things, in doubt, sometimes blindly.

**D · Main task — 6, The Lovers.** What the couple has to learn: to love a person, not an image; to choose with their own eyes, not someone else's; not to mistake love for jealousy, control and idealisation.

intro: This tail has a play in which it is acted out almost point by point: Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream. Two lovers run away into the forest at night: that is the entry. In the forest a magic flower confuses who chooses whom: that is the middle. In the morning everyone has to choose again, this time in front of others and in sunlight: that is the main task. What follows is an investigation — of what is written in the cards themselves, in the numbers of the couple's matrix and in the text of the play.

faq.q: Is the 18-6-6 tail a bad sign for a couple's compatibility?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not rate the union and does not predict how it will end. It shows a task: for 18-6-6 it is the road from love by moonlight — mystery, guesses, imagination — to choosing each other by daylight. The tail's difficulties are what the couple has to learn, not a verdict.

faq.q: Do The Lovers in a couple's tail mean infidelity or a rival?
faq.a: No. The Lovers do not prove that there is a third person in the couple. In A Midsummer Night's Dream the swaps are the flower's work, that is, the work of perception: each sees not a person but what they imagined. The tail's task lies exactly here — to see the partner, not an image.

faq.q: Does The Moon at the entry mean a partner is hiding something?
faq.a: No. The Moon at the entry to the task speaks of the couple's wish for a world of its own and of the language of hints the two speak. Its flip side is things left unsaid and guesses, but that is a habit shared by both, not one person's secret. Besides, neither partner brings The Moon to the entry: it is formed only from the two personal matrices.

faq.q: What can a couple with the 18-6-6 tail do?
faq.a: Talk the night through aloud: tell each other how each sees the beginning of the relationship and what is happening between them; turn guesses into questions; make small choices aloud and not measure themselves against other people's eyes. If jealousy turns into control, threats or fear, that is no longer the tail's task but a reason to see a psychologist, and in danger, to call a local emergency number or crisis line.

faq.q: How does the 18-6-6 couple tail differ from the personal 18-6-6 tail?
faq.a: A personal tail is worked out from one birth date and speaks about one person. A couple's tail is made up of two personal tails and speaks about a task that exists only for the two together. The numbers coincide; the roles of the points and the meaning differ.

report: In Shakespeare the middle of the task is a flower. Cupid took aim at a maiden in the west, "But I might see young Cupid's fiery shaft / Quench'd in the chaste beams of the watery moon" — and the arrow fell on a little flower. Love's arrow passed through moonlight and became a juice that changes what the eyes see. This is the tail's step from 18 to 6: The Lovers, having passed through The Moon. The flower is the wild pansy, and pansy comes from the French pensée, "thought"; in Russian it is anyutiny glazki, "Annie's little eyes". A thought dropped onto the eyes: falling in love has never been described more exactly.

The road of a couple with this tail runs through choice, and the choice is not made once: where to live, whose friends to spend Saturday with, whose side to take when a mother calls. By moonlight it sometimes gets tangled: yesterday the partner seemed the best person on earth; today, a stranger. After the night Hermia says: "Methinks I see these things with parted eye, / When every thing seems double." And Helena answers: "And I have found Demetrius like a jewel, / Mine own, and not mine own."

**"Mine own, and not mine own" is the formula of the tail's middle.** The partner is chosen but not owned. Jealousy, checking and suspicion grow exactly from the attempt to make "mine" what also remains "not mine". The swaps in the forest are the flower's work, that is, the work of perception: The Lovers in the tail do not mean a third person in the couple.

The morning begins with the Duke asking whether this is the day Hermia must give her answer. The main task is to choose, and the play shows what gets in the way. Other people's eyes: "O hell! to choose love by another's eyes." — a father in the play, a mother's "he's not the one" in life. Disbelief at being the one chosen: Helena says of herself "No, no, I am as ugly as a bear", and takes a declaration of love for mockery. Insecurity turned into control: Hermia, jealous, threatens her friend with her nails. An image instead of a person: the lover, Theseus says, "Sees Helen's beauty in a brow of Egypt".

The middle and the main task of this tail are one card. Lysander chooses Hermia twice: in Athens, under her window by moonlight, and in the morning after the forest, when the spell is lifted. It is the same person, but the second choice is made by daylight, after a night in which everything seemed double. **The hidden plot of 18-6-6 is not finding "the one" but choosing the one already chosen — now knowing them.** With Demetrius Shakespeare is bolder: his spell is never lifted, right to the end of the play. The play does not ask love to prove where it came from. It asks that a choice made at night be confirmed by day, aloud and in front of others.

report.h3: A night told by two becomes constancy

report: The way out of the tail hides in a line that readers usually skip. On waking, Demetrius calls the others to the temple: "And by the way let us recount our dreams." Theseus refuses to believe their story, and Hippolyta objects: "But all the story of the night told over, / And all their minds transfigured so together, / More witnesseth than fancy's images / And grows to something of great constancy." A night told over again, and together, grows into something very constant. Waite gives The Moon reversed the meaning "inconstancy". **Hippolyta names the opposite.**

ul: to tell each other the story of how it began — each their own version — and find where the versions differ;
to turn a guess into a question: not "that hurt" but "did that hurt?";
to call a bush a bush, aloud, and let the other answer;
to leave room in the couple for mystery and play, but not for silence about what matters;
to choose aloud, in small things, remembering that choosing each other is repeated, not done once and for all.

report: The strong version of this tail is a couple whose night has not been taken away but told: the mystery and the play remain, and the choice of each other has been made by daylight.

unit.title: Midsummer night's dream for two

captions.M: To want a world of your own that outsiders cannot enter
captions.N: To keep choosing each other, even when all seems double
captions.D: To choose the same person by daylight, knowing them

unit.meaning: Your task is to repeat by day the choice made at night: see each other, not an image, and turn guesses into questions.
